canberra.title: Man faces trial accused of committing beastiality on housemate’s cat
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article contains distressing content and alleged animal abuse. The defence lawyer for a man accused of committing a...
canberra.content:
A man, aged in his late-20s, is fighting a charge of beastiality in his Supreme Court trial. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

CONTENT WARNING: This article contains distressing content and alleged animal abuse.

The defence lawyer for a man accused of committing an act of beastiality on a cat has argued the prosecution’s case is nothing but “a collection of suspicious circumstances”.

The man, who is aged in his late-20s but is not named for legal reasons, was alleged to have abused his housemate’s cat, whose name is Dutch, at their home in Canberra in February 2025.

He pleaded not guilty to one count of beastiality in his ACT Supreme Court jury trial, which ran for about a day-and-a-half before closing addresses took place on Tuesday afternoon (18 August).

Prosecutor Sam McLaughlin told jurors the man and the housemate went out that night, before the man returned home first.

He said when the housemate came back, he found the man at the kitchen sink, tending to some injuries. The man told him Dutch had attacked him, but when the housemate challenged him on this account, the man broke down.

Mr McLaughlin said the housemate reported Dutch was normally playful, confident and “a bit of a rascal”. But after he returned home that night, the cat was crouching low, hissed at him and was “really, really pissed off”.

Mr McLaughlin said when the man and the housemate left home that evening, neither Dutch nor the man had any injuries, while Dutch, a strictly indoor cat, was left inside.

He said no one else lived at their home and the man was the first to return that night. Also, between the time the housemate left the home and returned, something happened to Dutch that caused injuries to his anus and made him “really, really pissed off”.

Mr McLaughlin said photos showed multiple significant scratches to the man’s hands and arms. He said jurors may think these injuries were consistent with the suggestion that they were caused by a cat while it was being held against its will.

The prosecutor also said two veterinarians reported the injuries on Dutch’s anus were likely caused by penetration.

But the man’s barrister, Edward Chen, said DNA test results showed there had been no human DNA inside Dutch’s rectum.

“This point in itself outweighs all the other evidence,” he said.

“This is a case about suspicion versus science.”

Mr Chen said an alternative hypothesis was that “something traumatic” happened to Dutch after his client and the housemate had gone out drinking that night.

He said his client returned home first, and perhaps there had been some kind of interaction that caused Dutch to attack him as the cat was already frightened and in a heightened state.

Mr Chen also said even if the jurors accepted the vets’ opinions that Dutch’s anus was penetrated, these opinions didn’t prove who caused the penetration.

“I suggest the true nature of the prosecution’s case is a collection of suspicious circumstances,” he said.

Chief Justice Lucy McCallum has begun summarising the case for the jury.

canberra.title: Calls for Wagga Council boss to resign after four dogs found dead at Wilks Park
canberra.snippet: A Wagga housing advocate has called for Wagga City Council general manager Peter Thompson to resign after four dogs returned to a homeles...
canberra.content:
The Shar Peis were living at Wilks Park. Photos: Supplied.

A Wagga housing advocate has called for Wagga City Council general manager Peter Thompson to resign after four dogs returned to a homeless man living at Wilks Park were found dead this week.

The dogs, believed to be Shar Peis, were collected from the park after their deaths, with the council confirming the animals had been found dead.

The deaths have prompted questions over why the dogs were returned to their owner after spending 11 days in council care at the Glenfield Road Animal Shelter.

Tim Verhoef, Chris Roche, Leigh Swansborough and Vickie Burkinshaw held a press conference on Tuesday (18 August), criticising the decision to return the dogs to the man.

Mr Roche told the media the dogs had been returned to someone he described as a “known animal hoarder”.

“Once again, the council and the State Government were being reactive, not proactive,” he said.

Mr Verhoef described the decision as “cruelty and incompetence”, and said the man had previously owned as many as 21 dogs.

“We tried to advocate for him, but no services will help him,” he said.

Mr Verhoef also questioned how the council could have returned the dogs given what advocates say they knew about the man’s circumstances.

“To release the dogs to someone who is a known animal hoarder – how can you give that order?”

He called for Mr Thompson to resign.

The advocates also said the situation highlighted broader failures in support for people experiencing homelessness and living with animals.

Ms Burkinshaw called for a more compassionate approach from the council.

“We are picking on the most vulnerable people in our community and acting with cruelty rather than supporting them in their transition to a pathway home,” she said.

Tim Verhoef speaking at the press conference.

Region asked the council to explain the circumstances surrounding the dogs’ death and the reasons they were returned to Wilks Park.

“The owner, who is living in a homelessness encampment at the site, owns as many as 15 dogs and has been approached on many occasions by council and agencies, including the RSPCA,” a spokesperson said.

“Council and the emergency task force have expressed constant concern about the number of dogs in this person’s care, their health and their living conditions, and has endeavoured to find solutions, all of which have been opposed by the owner.

“In recent weeks, four of the dogs were discovered roaming and unattended. They were picked up and taken to the animal shelter in accordance with ordinary practice.

“The dogs remained in care at the shelter for 11 days, where a qualified veterinarian visits the animal shelter every weekday to check on animal health.

“When the four dogs were seized, the owner was transported to the animal shelter by a community member, where he demanded the return of his dogs. They were not returned on this day because a fee needed to be paid for their return.

“The owner attended council workplaces each day over three days with escalating threats and abuse towards staff, demanding the return of the dogs. Upon the owner paying the fees, his dogs were returned to him as he was lawfully entitled to their return.”

The cause of the four dogs’ death has not been publicly detailed by the council.

The council has now taken the remaining dogs into its care at the Glenfield Road Animal Shelter.

The shelter is the council’s designated facility for lost and stray animals.

The advocates say the deaths should prompt a broader examination of how the council and government agencies respond to vulnerable people living with animals.

Original Article published by Oliver Jacques on Region Riverina.

canberra.title: Man accused of throat-slitting message ‘at a loss for words’ when refused bail
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged family violence. A man accused of threatening to kill his partner and blow up her mother&...
canberra.content:
A man has failed in his attempt to be released from custody after being accused of threatening to kill a woman. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged family violence.

A man accused of threatening to kill his partner and blow up her mother’s home said he was “at a loss for words” to learn he would be refused bail.

He represented himself when applying for bail in the ACT Magistrates Court on Tuesday (18 August), repeatedly confirming he was happy proceeding without his lawyer.

“I wasn’t even aware that I had court until they came and woke me up this morning,” he said, even though his bail application had been pre-listed as he had been in custody for about a month.

When proposing bail conditions, the man, in his mid-20s, offered to stay home under a curfew and report to a police station six times a week, just not on Sundays.

“As I am a Christian man, your honour, I reserve Sundays for the Lord,” he said.

The court heard he had been accused of sending threatening messages to the woman, as well as leaving a voicemail in which he referred to slitting somebody’s throat.

Prosecutor Madeleine Gallo, who opposed bail, said the woman reported she would be “terrified” if the man was released from custody.

The woman alleged he had made multiple threats to kill her, to blow up her mother’s house and to send people to her own home.

“I’m simply not a threat,” the man said.

“I don’t know where she’s got that from.”

The court was adjourned for a time for the man to read documents that outlined the allegations against him. When he came back, he admitted: “They’re actually quite confronting and heinous”.

But he reiterated, “I haven’t said any of this”.

The man said he was an event cleaner for Summernats, which is a festival that is held in January.

“I do have work,” he said.

“There’s no reason why, in my eyes, bail should be opposed.”

Ms Gallo said there was a “brazenness” to the allegations, as the man was alleged to have explicitly told the woman he didn’t care about being reported to police.

Magistrate Glenn Theakston said when the man was arrested, he appeared to use similar language with the police officers as he was alleged to have used with the woman.

The magistrate said the content of the messages the man was alleged to have sent was “confronting” and he refused bail.

When the man responded to the comments about how he acted when police arrived at this home to arrest him, he claimed he had significant post-traumatic stress disorder due to how police had treated him in the past.

“I’m at a loss for words, it’s unfortunate,” he said.

The man, who has not been named to protect the woman’s identity, has been charged with four counts of using a carriage service to threaten, as well as two counts of using a carriage service to menace, harass or cause offence.

The matter was adjourned to 24 August. No pleas have been entered.

canberra.title: Controversial Hume Circle rezoning referred to federal inquiry
canberra.snippet: The controversial rezoning of land around Hume Circle to allow apartment buildings up to 15 storeys tall has been referred to a parliamen...
canberra.content:
The Hume Circle roundabout, around which major development will now be possible. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

The controversial rezoning of land around Hume Circle to allow apartment buildings up to 15 storeys tall has been referred to a parliamentary committee inquiry.

Regional Development, Local Government and Territories Minister Kristy McBain has written to the Chair of the Joint Standing Committee on the National Capital and External Territories requesting the establishment of an inquiry into National Capital Plan Amendment No. 102 – Hume Circle Precinct.

Ms McBain approved the amendment earlier this month after the National Capital Authority revised its proposal in response to community opposition.

A spokesperson for Ms McBain said the referral acknowledged the high level of community interest in the amendment, which opens the way for the precinct to become one of the densest in Canberra.

The inquiry would consider the National Capital Authority’s consultation process; the different stages of high-level strategic planning and whether this process can be improved; and the long-term planning approach for community infrastructure, open space, transport and utilities for the precinct.

A Steering Committee, comprising representatives from the NCA and relevant ACT Government agencies, was already being established to support a coordinated approach to future planning for the precinct.

Committee member and ACT Senator David Pocock welcomed the referral, saying the NCA needed to rebuild trust with Canberrans after the way it initially conducted community consultation on this project.

Senator Pocock has been calling for an inquiry for weeks and said it would provide greater transparency, help rebuild trust and allow issues to be canvassed in detail.

Building heights will vary across the Hume Circle Precinct. 15 storeys will be allowed at selected sites, subject to certain conditions. Image: NCA.

The NCA, which has been talking with development consortium Jega since 2023, proposed DA102 in January, arguing that it would revitalise the areas around the Hume Circle roundabout bordered by Narrabundah, Griffith, Kingston and Fyshwick.

It also said it would restore the original Griffin plan for a radial street system and eastern gateway to Canberra.

But the proposal was lashed as rewriting history by a Griffin expert and attacked by community groups and existing residents for the scale of development it would unleash.

Even the ACT Government was alarmed at the density it would allow and the infrastructure it would require.

In response, the NCA scaled back the density, although 15 storeys will still be possible in selected sites, and included more planning detail and requirements.

Senator Pocock said these were welcome, but the proposal still lacked much of the detail seen in previous amendments to the NCP.

He contrasted planning for the Hume Circle Precinct with that for Constitution Avenue.

“Constitution Avenue included indicative cycleways, integrated urban art and signage, car parking, building height and form, active frontage, indicative streetscape design, indicative road structure, public transport pathways, access and circulation and indicative main pedestrian connections,” he said.

The Territory Planning Authority and the Suburban Land Agency had raised red flags about the impact on the nearby East Lake Urban Renewal Project, population densities that would require matching infrastructure and services – such as schools, shops, roads and utilities – and a lack of provision for open space.

canberra.title: One Nation has plans to stub out the illicit tobacco trade
canberra.snippet: One Nation has a solution to Australia’s illegal tobacco trade, and that’s for the Federal Government to slash the tobacco excise so peop...
canberra.content:
Illicit tobacco seized in Victoria last year. The current excise is just over $38 per pack of 25, or $1.53 per cigarette. Photo: Australian Federal Police.

One Nation has a solution to Australia’s illegal tobacco trade, and that’s for the Federal Government to slash the tobacco excise so people will start buying legal cigarettes again.

Pauline Hanson briefly outlined her party’s new policy on Tuesday (18 August), to cut the tobacco excise by 75 per cent and put a hold on indexation for three years.

Senator Hanson said the current management of tobacco sales has failed and only served to give a “multi-billion-dollar market to organised crime”.

She has found little love for the idea so far, with Labor saying law enforcement should be the priority, the Coalition insisting it has a better plan, and the Greens blasting One Nation for pushing big tobacco’s agenda.

One Nation’s Barnaby Joyce, however, said the minor party’s plan was just common sense; that the price of legal cigarettes should be lowered to match that of the illicit tobacco products.

“This is just absurd economics that if you keep on putting up the price of cigarettes you are going to get more excise,” Senator Joyce said.

“No. If you keep on putting up the price of cigarettes, you’re going to get more mafia. That’s what you’re getting, more mafia.

“The only way we can deal with the criminality, the mafia that also underwrites so many other drugs, is to bring back the price of legal cigarettes to the same realm as where illegal ones are.”

Tobacco excise has risen in Australia by more than 200 per cent over the past decade. A legal pack of cigarettes now costs around $65.

The current excise is just over $38 per pack of 25, or $1.53 per cigarette.

Slashing it would bring down the price of a pack by about $30, making it closer to the far cheaper illicit smokes imported from Asia and the Middle East.

Australian Bureau of Statistics data suggests about 80 per cent of tobacco products and vapes currently purchased are illegal.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers says the government has no plans to reduce the excise but acknowledges that illicit trade presents a serious challenge.

“For the government, our primary focus has been on providing hundreds of millions of dollars in extra resources for the police and other authorities to crack down on this big problem in our society and in local communities as well,” he said.

“Now, we’ve had some recent successes when it comes to that crackdown.

“We’ve seen some raids and some busts when it comes to some of this illegal supply. That’s a good thing. We want to see more of that.”

Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson said the Opposition would like to tackle the tobacco excise, but Labor is in the way.

“In principle, we want to cut out the black market and the organised crime that the Albanese government has let fester,” he said.

“What we know is, through pride, the Albanese government is ruling out any measure that would stomp down on organised crime, which is literally handing over the trade to criminals that’s then going on to do things like finance terrorism and hurt the Australian community.

“It’s time the Albanese government got past its pride, acknowledged, just like in their budget, that adding more taxes doesn’t always deliver, or definitely doesn’t deliver, better outcomes for the Australian people.”

Nationals leader Matt Canavan says the Coalition is open to cutting the excise, but he’s not going for One Nation’s plan, describing it as a thought bubble.

“I am critical of what has been, in the last week, a thought bubble upon thought bubble approach to policy from One Nation,” Senator Canavan said.

“Bubbles are fascinating, but they eventually pop.

“What we will do is come forward with a policy on vaping, on excise, on all these policy areas, that last.

“We will come forward with a very detailed, considered policy.”

Greens leader Larissa Waters was scathing of the One Nation policy, and accused Senator Hanson of toadying up to the tobacco lobby.

“It’s pretty clear that Pauline Hanson is doing precisely what big tobacco have been lobbying her to do,” she said.

“We see them haunting the halls of parliament here, trying to boost their profits.

“I mean, if you want to fight crime, fight crime. But don’t dress up fighting crime as just a premise to boost the profits of big tobacco.

“Anything that Philip Morris wants to do primarily revolves around them boosting their own profits off the pain of humans and the cancer and the devastation that they will wreak.

“So I don’t have a lot of sympathy for big tobacco, and I don’t think they should be influencing our politics.”

australia.title: Family of missing 18-year-old hiker ‘absolutely devastated’ as search continues in rugged NSW terrain
australia.snippet: Lily Hooper has not been seen since leaving for a hike in Nattai national park, south-west of Sydney, on 12 August Get our breaking news ...
australia.content:
The family of missing 18-year-old bushwalker Lily Hooper say they are “absolutely devastated” that she hasn’t been found after a multi-agency search.

On Tuesday, search efforts for the teenager continued through the dense tree canopy and rugged terrain of Nattai national park, about 90km south-west of Sydney, for a seventh day.

“Our family is absolutely devastated that our beloved daughter Lily is missing,” the family said in a statement on Tuesday afternoon. “We desperately want to bring Lily home safe and we ask as the search continues, to keep our family and Lily in your thoughts.”

Hooper left her Sydney home on Wednesday 12 August for a hike. Initial police inquiries indicate she reached the summit of Bonnum Pic mountain mid-morning on Wednesday, having sent messages from the trail earlier that day.

She was reported missing when she did not return home that evening. Her car was located by emergency services near the trail head on Wanganderry Road at High Range at 11pm on Wednesday.

As of Tuesday afternoon, police said no trace of Hooper or her belongings had been found.

On Monday, police said the search would focus on the lower sections of the Bonnum Pic walking trail.

NSW police chief inspector Brendan Bernie confirmed on Monday that thermal and aerial sweeps by PolAir late on Sunday evening were unsuccessful.

“We’ve just found no trace of Lily,” he said. “It’s quite dense with the bushland and there’s a dense tree canopy which also hinders our aerial searching.”

Police were uncertain of what supplies Hooper had with her, he said.

“We’re hopefully relying on Lily’s experience to get her through this ordeal and can locate her safely.”

Poor weather over the weekend hampered search operations in the already complex terrain.

“We would like to thank all the emergency services and volunteers for their support and continued commitment to the search, not only during the day but throughout the night,” the Hooper family said on Tuesday.

They also thanked those who offered to help search, but said due to “terrain and conditions we ask just professional search teams continue”.

The search team now includes PolAir, NSW Police Rescue, the SES, RFS, Fire and Rescue NSW, and National Parks and Wildlife Service. Volunteers on the ground include Hooper’s friends, family and Volunteer Rescue Association crews mobilised from as far north as Cessnock.

The family asked for privacy and understanding as they navigated the “unimaginable situation”.

Hooper is described as Caucasian, approximately 175cm tall, of slim build, with long blond hair and blue eyes. She was last seen wearing a shirt and shorts.

Anyone with information or who walked the Bonnum Pic trail on Wednesday is urged to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000.

    Welcome

What we learned today, Tuesday 18 August

What a jam-packed day for news from our nation’s capital!

Before we go, let’s recap the day’s top headlines:

  • The government and Coalition have reached deals on gambling reforms and the NDIS bill.

  • Labor’s Andrew Charlton advised Australia should adopt AI “everywhere we can”, in a speech to the Australian National University this morning.

  • Charlton also dismissed media reports of NAB warning that rents in Sydney and Melbourne could rise by up to 30% due to budget changes to negative gearing and the capital gains tax discount.

  • The Australian federal police told the shadow defence minister, James Paterson, that it will review the leak of a memo sent by Japanese diplomats to the Australian government over melon-gate.

  • Barnaby Joyce says increasing the tobacco excise, which makes legal cigarettes more expensive is just leading to “more mafia” around the country, as he argues that the excise should be cut.

  • The Northern Territory Wagering Commission, which regulates almost all online gambling operators in Australia, is yet to contact any bookmaker in response to Luke Bateman’s allegations before a Senate inquiry earlier this month.

  • The Australian cricketer David Warner was convicted and fined $1,500 for mid-range drink-driving after he tried to switch seats with a passenger when approaching a random breath-testing site on Easter Sunday.

  • For those who missed it, here’s what happened in question time.

Thanks for sticking around, we’ll see you tomorrow morning.

Severe weather warnings in place for northern Victoria

Jack Larkin

Flood warnings are in place in northern Victoria, with heavy rainfall predicted to extend across the state and into South Australia and New South Wales on Wednesday.

As of Tuesday afternoon, Bureau of Meteorology flood warnings were in place for Barham, Quambatook, McCoys Bridge, Bandiana and Appin South in northern Victoria.

David Crock, a senior meteorologist with the bureau, said to expect rain across northern Victoria and north-eastern Victoria: “we’re expecting a further 15 to 25 millimetres of rain … with a few spots probably getting to 30 or 40 millimetres”.

Crock said people near the Goulburn, Avoca and Loddon rivers should keep an eye on the water level. He said:

The rivers are wet. They will respond really quickly to further rainfall. So we may see some more flood warnings over the next few days across northern Victoria, depending on how much rainfall.

The weather system is expected to extend down to northern Tasmania, where there is also expected to be a flood risk.

Josh Butler

Gambling changes ‘complex’ and ‘unnecessary’, wagering industry warns

The peak body for online wagering companies has criticised the amendments on Labor’s gambling bill, claiming the changes would “further drive those at risk of gambling harm into the hands of criminal cartels running illegal offshore gambling sites”.

Responsible Wagering Australia – which represents Sportsbet and other major betting companies – claimed that cracking down on inducements would see punters go to overseas companies, which would offer bonus bets and other promotions. RWA said:

The deal done between the government and the opposition disregards that risk, and undermines the positive measures aimed at addressing the offshore market.

The bills will already significantly reduce visibility of Australian licensed brands, and by adding administratively complex, broadly drafted measures to further reduce advertising and customer promotions, offshore providers are expected to swoop on vulnerable punters.

CEO Kai Cantwell claimed the changes would “significantly curtail our ability to advertise a legal product safely to adults”. He also called out the “complexities” of the new one-stop opt-out register, questioning how it would work.

David Pocock to vote against gambling legislation in Senate

The independent senator David Pocock has criticised amendments to the government’s gambling reform bill, saying the legislation and its amendments fail on gambling ads.

Speaking on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, he called the bill “a betrayal of all Australians”.

We’ve got vested interests exerting pressure on the major parties, and the major parties doing a deal to put the gambling industry, free-to-air television and the major sporting codes ahead of Australians and our children.

We will still see three ads an hour on free-to-air television, and kids will still see gambling ads.

Pocock, who played a key role in the recent Senate inquiry into the government’s gambling legislation, said he planned to vote against the bill.

We have this opportunity as a parliament to implement evidence-based policy and actually treat gambling as the public health issue it is. We have a prime minister who tries to tell us that somehow getting the balance right is more important than doing the right thing.

David Warner fined $1,500 after being convicted of drink-driving

The Australian cricketer David Warner was convicted and fined $1,500 on Tuesday for mid-range drink-driving after he tried to switch seats with a passenger when approaching a random breath-testing site on Easter Sunday, AAP reports.

The 39-year-old’s barrister argued he should be spared conviction for the offence – when he blew more than twice the legal limit – because he had suffered extra punishment as a result of media coverage.

Awais Ahmad told Waverley local court his client’s indiscretion had been covered in global outlets including ESPN, Al Jazeera and the Indian Express.

Countries including India and Bangladesh, where Warner might be seeking to play in T20 franchise leagues, have an acceptance of a “non-drinking culture”, Ahmad said.

The consequences of his offending are profound.

Commercial opportunities [are] being affected.

Warner was arrested while he was on an Easter trip home from the subcontinent, where he captained the Karachi Kings in the Pakistan Super League.

When Warner saw the breath-testing site, he stopped short and attempted to swap seats with a female passenger, the agreed facts read out in court state.

Once police identified him as the driver, he cooperated with the testing, Judge Clare Farnan noted.

Ahmad questioned the decision of NSW police to issue a press release about Warner’s arrest given the unremarkable nature of the offence.

“The media onslaught thereafter has been quite profound,” the lawyer said.

Farnan said there was evidence of cruel social media commentary directed at Warner and his wife, Candice Warner.

His position as captain of the Sydney Thunder in the domestic Big Bash League was also under threat, the cricketer’s lawyer said.

The Thunder, along with rival Sydney Sixers and Sheffield Shield team the NSW Blues, are part of a state government campaign to deter drink-driving.

Despite the star batter’s pleas, Farnan said the need to deter the public from drink-driving was paramount in her decision to convict him.

The offence was aggravated because children were in the car at the time, the judge said.

Warner will be able to drive after he applies for an interlock licence and has the device fitted to his car.

The interlock will prevent the car from starting if it detects alcohol in his system.

Two people charged with murder after human remains allegedly found on suburban property

Two people have been charged with murder after a missing person’s remains were allegedly found on a suburban property, AAP reports.

Courtenay Williams, 52, and Carlie Rochelle Mordue, 45, have been accused of murdering Chad Steven Bishop, more than four years after he went missing.

The duo were also charged with interfering with a corpse after human remains were allegedly found during a police search of a Bethania property south of Brisbane on Monday.

Williams, a chippy, and Mordue, who works in sales, were not required to appear in Brisbane magistrates court on Tuesday when their cases were briefly mentioned for the first time.

Police allege they murdered Bishop in a Beenleigh townhouse on or about 2 March 2022, according to court documents.

A three-week adjournment was sought by Williams’s solicitor on Tuesday.

Mordue’s solicitor also sought an adjournment for her client.

Magistrate Belinda Merrin adjourned both cases to 7 September at Brisbane magistrates court.

Williams and Mordue were both remanded in custody.

Gambling regulator hasn’t contacted bookmakers after Luke Bateman’s allegations

Henry Belot

The Northern Territory Wagering Commission, which regulates almost all online gambling operators in Australia, is yet to contact any bookmaker in response to Luke Bateman’s allegations before a Senate inquiry earlier this month.

The former rugby league star alleged gambling company promoters supplied him with cocaine and alcohol, telling a parliamentary inquiry the betting industry exercised no duty of care. He also told the inquiry he attended a private Gold Coast event hosted by a gambling company at which senior figures allegedly took illicit drugs with clients.

Bateman did not name any specific companies, but betting giants Sportsbet and Tabcorp told the inquiry there was no evidence its account managers sourced drugs and sex workers to incentivise vulnerable people to bet more.

A commission spokesperson said it was reviewing the Senate inquiry’s report, tabled on Monday, and was considering “whether any of the matters raised warrant further regulatory consideration”. They said Bateman’s allegations were “untested”:

The Commission would treat very seriously any allegation that a NT licensed operator was involved in the provision of illegal drugs to customers or failed to comply with the requirement in the Code to prevent intoxicated customers from gambling.

The Commission notes that there have been no specific allegations by Mr Bateman concerning NT licensed operators. No contact has been made with NT licensed operators at this stage.

The Commission will consider the reporting in the context of its regulatory responsibilities before determining whether any further action is appropriate.

Josh Butler

Coalition says news bargaining code won’t help enough journalists

The Coalition says the news bargaining incentive (NBI) isn’t strong enough to support Australian media, with the shadow minister, Sarah Henderson, worried it could take journalists “backwards” from current arrangements.

The NBI is levelled at online giants like Google, Meta and TikTok, and designed to compensate mainstream news outlets for the value of their content and support public interest journalism. The legislation is yet to pass parliament, but those companies will have to pay 2.5% of their Australian digital advertising revenue.

The Coalition has agreed to back the NBI, but Henderson said she still had concerns. She said:

We’re not convinced that it’s at the right place … we are concerned that under the government’s proposal, that potentially takes media companies and, of course, the journalists that media companies support backwards. We don’t want to see those deals go backwards, and so we want to see more in the pot for Australian journalism, which is so important for our democracy.

We want to see the digital platforms being held to account, and that’s why we will be looking very closely at that bill and agitating for some further changes.

Asked if that 2.5% figure should be higher, Henderson said: “we will be prosecuting the need for more money to go into the pot rather than less.”

Labor loses Senate vote, motion condemns ‘flawed’ aged care tool

Josh Butler

Labor continues to come under intense scrutiny over its new aged care assessment tool, with the government losing a vote in the Senate as the entire non-Labor cohort of senators backed a Greens motion slamming the new tool.

The Greens senator Penny Allman-Payne moved a motion a short time ago, which stated that the Integrated Assessment Tool (IAT) “is untested, structurally flawed and systematically under-assessing the care needs of older Australians, especially those living with mental health conditions, cognitive issues and frailty”.

The motion called on the government to “take immediate action to abolish the IAT” and replace it with a new tool “designed with clinical experts”. The Greens motion also demanded the government ensures the system guarantees “the rights of older people as its first priority and restore the role of clinical professionals in the assessment process and reinstate the ability for human override”.

Labor opposed the motion. But the Greens, Liberals and crossbench all backed it. It passed 34 votes to 23, with only Labor senators voting against it. It is essentially only a symbolic motion, and does not require the government to take any action, but shows the depth of anger in the parliament at the controversial change.

‘Will pass the Senate tonight’: Labor confident on NDIS bill

The federal health minister, Mark Butler, says the government is confident its NDIS bill will pass parliament by the end of today.

Speaking at a press conference, Butler said the government had reached an amendments agreement with the Coalition to secure the bill’s passage through the Senate.

I’m confident [the bill] will pass the Senate tonight. The bill will be substantially amended, with 33 amendments in the Senate, following the 30 amendments that we supported in the House of Representatives.

Some are relatively technical, but some are relatively substantial as well. They will ensure that this bill is the best version it can be.

Speaking beside him, the NDIS minister, Jenny McAllister, said the bill’s passage would be the product of “listening to people across parliament”.

I acknowledge colleagues in the Coalition, in particular the shadow minister. They have taken a constructive approach to these negotiations. So today, we do have an agreement to pass these reforms and I believe that they will deliver an NDIS which is strong, safe, sustainable and has a strong social licence.

Krishani Dhanji

Thank you all for joining me on the live blog today!

I’ll leave you with the lovely Achol Arok and see you here bright and early tomorrow.

One-stop shop for gambling ad opt-out was the Coalition’s idea, Henderson says

The shadow communications minister, Sarah Henderson, says despite criticism from her own side that the gambling bill is still “weak” the Coalition are “really pleased that our amendments have significantly strengthened this bill”.

She also says that she was “disappointed” to see Anika Wells claim the one-stop shop to opt-out from gambling ads.

We’re very disappointed that the communications minister went into the House yesterday and claimed that as her own. That was very much a proposal of the Coalition.

Speaking to the media after question time, Henderson says the bill removes predatory inducements against people who are “red flagged” by gambling companies, and is happy about the three-year review.

Asked if that review means she sees this legislation as unfinished business, Henderson answers:

The statutory review is an important part of this process. We want to see accountability, we want to see transparency, and that’s what the statutory review does deliver.

Tl;dr here’s what happened in question time

  • The Coalition attacked the government on housing, after NAB reportedly warned rents could increase up to 30% (the PM said the bank had later clarified and confirmed it wasn’t a forecast).

  • The veterans’ affairs minister, Matt Keogh, apologised for initially refusing an invitation to meet with veterans in Canberra, before bowing to political pressure. Keogh continued to feel the heat with an additional question on whether the government would scrap a cap on allied health service support for veterans.

  • The independent MP Rebekha Sharkie asked if the government would force gambling companies to fund regional community sports infrastructure.

  • Independent Allegra Spender pushed the aged care minister on Labor’s controversial algorithm-based aged care assessment tool.

  • And Tim Wilson, with just minutes to spare on question time, was booted out of the chamber for interjecting too much.

After a final dixer to the agriculture minister, Julie Collins, the PM calls time on QT.

Anthony Albanese and the deputy Nationals leader, Darren Chester, thank Collins for her work to combat bird flu before MPs leave the chamber.

australia.title: Victoria moves to expand definition of ‘corruption’ before state election
australia.snippet: Former Ibac head welcomes potential change that could capture actions that currently cannot be used to make corrupt findings Get our brea...
australia.content:
Ben Carroll has committed to changing the definition of “corruption” before the Victorian election in a move a former anti-corruption boss says could have captured the conduct of senior government figures had it been in place earlier.

The Victorian premier announced on Tuesday said it was his intention to introduce the legislation – which will expand the jurisdiction of the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission (Ibac) – before the government enters caretaker mode in November.

Carroll also said he was “very close” to releasing the terms of reference for a royal commission into the construction sector, which Guardian Australia understands could happen within days.

The Victorian parliament will sit for additional days to accommodate for the Ibac legislation and to establish a special prosecutor to work in parallel with the royal commission’s investigation.

“We are working very hard in terms of broad terms of reference to shine a light on what occurred, getting the best candidate to be commissioner,” Carroll said.

“[We are] also making sure we have lasting change [by] establishing an office for a special prosecutor and also the work the special minister of state continues to do not just on the royal commission, but giving our integrity agencies – in particular Ibac – the powers it needs and deserves.”

The special minister of state, Ingrid Stitt, said her department had been working to “bring forward” follow-the-dollar powers, allowing Ibac to investigate the spending of public money by private contractors and subcontractors, alongside a broader definition of corrupt conduct.

“The premier has been very clear that he wants these powers to be in the parliament and hopefully passed in this term of government,” Stitt said.

Currently, Ibac can only investigate suspected corruption that constitutes a relevant criminal offence. It also is unable to make findings of corrupt conduct unless the conduct constitutes a relevant criminal offence.

A parliamentary inquiry into the adequacy of Victoria’s integrity framework, tabled in December, said it received many submissions that described the threshold as too narrow, as it failed to capture “grey corruption” and other breaches of public trust.

It recommended that the threshold be changed to capture behaviour that could included committing a disciplinary offence, misconduct worthy of termination, or instances considered in breach of public trust by a public officer.

It also recommended giving Ibac the power to make and publish formal findings of corrupt conduct. The government had accepted the recommendations in principle.

The former Ibac commissioner Robert Redlich, who now chairs the Accountability Round Table, said such changes would bring Ibac jurisdiction closer to that of the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption.

“Everyone understands when a public servant receives a bribe – when money goes into their pocket as a result of what they do or fail to do – that’s a crime. But as soon as you have public servants acting for other improper purposes but which don’t personally benefit them, then you’re immediately in that grey area,” he said.

“It doesn’t necessarily fit into conduct that merits criminal conduct, which is one of the fundamental reasons why that higher threshold has been so problematic.”

Redlich said the combination of a broader definition and follow-the-dollar powers would mean there would be “no inhibitions” on Ibac to investigate allegations of corruption on the Victorian government’s Big Build infrastructure program.

Redlich said the changes could have also affected the findings of Operation Richmond, which was tabled in parliament earlier this month.

The report stopped short of making any findings of corrupt conduct. But it found senior members of the Andrews government engaged in “serious and concerning” conduct in their dealings with Peter Marshall, the secretary of the United Firefighters Union.

This included “actions contrary to policy, procedure and codes of conduct, deliberate attempts to conceal and mislead, and the misuse of information”.

“Given the findings of breaches in conventions and standards it appears probable that the misconduct would meet the definition of the lower threshold of corruption,” Redlich said of the Ibac’s report into the matter.

Catherine Williams, from the Centre for Public Integrity, welcomed the prospect of reform before the election.

“It’s been a long-lamented limitation because it has meant that the state doesn’t have a fit for purpose integrity commission,” she said.

But she warned Ibac would need additional resources to “fulfil its mandate”.

australia.title: David Pocock condemns Labor-Coalition deal on gambling bill as ‘betrayal of all Australians’
australia.snippet: Labor’s legislation to restrict gambling ads is set to pass this week, with the Greens calling the agreement ‘cowardly’ Get our breaking ...
australia.content:
Two Coalition MPs have crossed the floor after a deal between the major parties to pass Labor’s new restrictions on betting advertising and inducements, with crossbenchers and the Greens expressing anger and dismay at the contentious bill’s final form.

Anthony Albanese and the communications minister, Anika Wells, secured the support of the opposition to pass the bill, with amendments including tweaks to ad timing rules and some restrictions on inducements.

Wells called the package “the most significant reforms to online gambling in Australia’s history”. Albanese, in a speech to parliament, thanked the Coalition for its support and called the reforms “a result that will work”.

The independent senator David Pocock condemned the deal, calling it a “betrayal of all Australians” on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing. He said he would be voting against the bills in the Senate and derided the amendments as “tinkering” that didn’t go nearly far enough.

The reforms are set pass on Thursday, 1,149 days after the late Labor MP Peta Murphy handed down her landmark report on gambling harms, which recommended a total ban on inducements and wagering ads.

Labor’s final version of the bill, with amendments agreed by the Coalition, will not meet either of those recommendations. Instead, the communications regulator will set up a one-stop “opt-out register” – the details and design of which is yet to be made clear – to allow Australians to elect against receiving gambling ads, while inducements will only be limited in some circumstances.

The register could take up to 12 months to be set up, government sources said, conceding the system would be complex and unlikely to be ready by 1 January 2027. Albanese referred to the system as “AdStop” in parliament, likening it to the self-exclusion register BetStop, but it’s understood this will not be its official name.

Gambling industry sources questioned how the opt-out register would operate, how long it would take to set up, as well as privacy issues around handling of user data. Wagering companies – who will be obliged to pay for the register – also questioned how much it would cost.

The shadow communications minister, Sarah Henderson, said the register idea had come from the Coalition.

She said the Coalition envisioned that “anyone seeking to serve gambling ads online will be required to sweep that register to make sure that if someone opts out on the register, that all publishers of gambling ads will comply with the law.”

Wells said all inducement ads would be banned for any customer “identified as at risk of gambling-related harm”, for 14 days after someone had signed up with a wagering service, and for three months after someone had deregistered from Betstop.

Tuesday’s amendments would also ban commissions on customer losses for gambling staff or affiliates.

“We have listened to the range of views across the community and the parliament, which showed us the most toxic version of inducements – and we are taking action to address this,” Wells said.

Kai Cantwell, CEO of the peak body Responsible Wagering Australia, described the changes as “unnecessary” and “complex”.

“If you push people away from the licensed, regulated market – by banning or limiting the promotions that let local operators compete, or by making Australian odds less competitive with new taxes and levies – you don’t stop them punting,” Cantwell said.

“You push them offshore, into products with no consumer protections, no support, no Betstop, and no contribution to Australian sport and racing.”

Other tweaks to the original bill include extending the “blackout period” on ads before live sport from five minutes to 15 minutes, the three-per-hour restriction on TV ads beginning at 5am instead of 6am, and restrictions on advertising during children’s programming.

The changes will be monitored by the Australian Communications and Media Authority and subject to a statutory review after three years.

Labor’s changes include previously announced reforms like banning gambling ads on player jerseys and in stadiums, banning celebrities and players from promoting gambling, and a “triple lock” system for online ads requiring users to be over 18, logged in and provided with an opt-out option.

The Liberal backbencher Andrew Wallace joined colleague Pat Conaghan to cross the floor and vote against some of the amendments, which he claimed were inadequate.

Wallace said the parliament should have extended advertising blackout periods, and an opt-in approach for inducements.

“These reforms don’t go anywhere near enough to correcting those bad elements. We’re putting too much faith in the hands of the gambling companies. And quite frankly, they have not demonstrated that they deserve that faith,” he told ABC TV.

Conaghan, who was deputy chair of the Murphy-led review in 2023, said earlier: “I think we’re being weak by not implementing those reports and I think we’d be supported by the majority of the public out there.”

Guardian Australia understands at least two more Liberal senators – moderates Andrew McLachlan and Paul Scarr – may cross the floor when the bill reaches the upper house tomorrow.

Independent Zali Steggall complained during debate that crossbenchers had not been given any time to consider amendments.

“Labor and the Coalition stitched up a deal on gambling laws then gave crossbench MPs just minutes to consider significant amendments before being expected to vote on them,” she said in a statement with colleague Allegra Spender.

The Greens called the Labor-Coalition agreement “cowardly and careless”.

Kate Seselja, co-chair of the group Gambling Harm Lived Experience Experts, said in a statement that the government should instead follow the recommendations of Murphy’s report.

“The only way to effectively block gambling ads is to ban them in Australia. This proposal is completely unworkable,” Seselja said of the universal “opt-out” register.

australia.title: Mushroom murderer Erin Patterson was convicted over three deaths. Now she’ll argue the court got it wrong
australia.snippet: An Australian court will consider two appeals from Wednesday: whether Patterson’s convictions should be quashed, and if she should remain...
australia.content:
It was a Sunday lunch in a sleepy Australian town that was at the heart of one of the country’s most high-profile murder trials.

A central question fascinated people around the world: did Erin Patterson deliberately serve her in-laws poisoned beef wellingtons on 29 July 2023?

More than a year after a jury found Patterson had murdered her in-laws, an Australian court will consider whether her convictions should be quashed and if she should remain in prison for life without the possibility of parole.

On Wednesday, three judges of Victoria’s highest court will begin hearing two appeals – by Patterson herself and the state’s director of public prosecutions (DPP) – in the triple-murder case that attracted worldwide intrigue and intense media attention for months.

Patterson will appeal against her convictions, while the DPP will appeal against the sentence handed down to Patterson, arguing it is “manifestly inadequate”.

In September, Patterson was sentenced to life imprisonment, with a non-parole period of 33 years, for the murders of her estranged husband’s parents – Don and Gail Patterson and his aunt, Heather Wilkinson. She was also convicted of the attempted murder of Heather’s husband, Ian Wilkinson, who survived the lunch after spending weeks in hospital.

Patterson, who maintained her innocence throughout the 11-week trial last year, is not expected to attend court in person. The three court of appeal judges, who will consider the arguments, are expected to reserve their decision in both appeals. They will hand down their judgments at a later date.

Patterson to appeal on seven grounds

In November, Patterson, 51, filed an appeal against her convictions but did not appeal against her sentence.

The appeal is on seven grounds including the “fundamental irregularity” around sequestering the jury in the same hotel as police and media representatives, and that her cross-examination during the trial was “unfair and oppressive”.

While considering the verdict, the jury was sequestered in a hotel in a regional town where police and members of the media also stayed. According to media reports, the matter was raised with authorities by her lawyers at the time, but no concerns about the process were raised during the trial.

The appeal documents allege the sequestering issue “fatally undermined the integrity of the verdicts” and argue for the quashing of the convictions and the ordering of a re-trial.

Patterson is also appealing on the grounds that cell tower evidence – along with evidence of death cap mushroom sightings near her home – should not have been heard in the trial. The court last year heard that analysis of Patterson’s mobile phone records revealed she may have visited two locations soon after death cap mushroom sightings were reported.

She is also arguing evidence from her Facebook “friends”, who met Patterson through a true-crime group, should not have been allowed as it was not “relevant”. Patterson told a Facebook group chat that she wanted “nothing to do” with her parents-in-law, according to messages shown in court.

The other four grounds of appeal relate to Patterson’s cross-examination by prosecutors over five days, along with issues over other evidence, and the opening and closing addresses of the prosecution.

Patterson’s legal team is arguing the prosecution’s closing address caused a “substantial miscarriage of justice”. While the prosecution maintained there was no evidence of motive, Patterson’s legal team claims, this changed in the closing address to imply a motive for murder.

If Patterson is successful in her appeal, the court will quash her convictions and could order a retrial or acquit her.

Prosecution: sentence ‘manifestly inadequate’

Separately, the DPP is appealing against Patterson’s sentence, arguing that “the sentence imposed on Patterson is manifestly inadequate”, and that the trial judge erred in finding she was likely to spend “years to come” in solitary confinement when allowing for the possibility of parole.

During a pre-sentencing hearing last August, the DPP argued Patterson should not be granted a parole period because of the nature of her crimes, which the judge, Justice Christopher Beale, agreed were “horrendous”.

While the defence and prosecution agreed that Patterson should receive a life sentence for the murders, her then defence barrister, Colin Mandy SC, argued she should receive a non-parole period. Mandy argued Beale should consider the onerous conditions of her conditions in custody.

At the time of the pre-sentence hearing in August 2025, Patterson had effectively spent the past 15 months in solitary confinement, the court heard.

Beale found that Patterson would continue to be held in those conditions for years to come for her own protection due to the high-profile nature of her crimes.

If the DPP’s appeal is successful, Patterson’s non-parole period could be extended or she could be sentenced to life without parole, with no option for release.

No further documentation has been released to the media since the two appeals were lodged last year. This includes the written cases relating to the appeal.

During Patterson’s 11-week trial, the prosecution did not put forward an alleged motive but pointed to the deteriorating relationship between Patterson and her estranged husband, Simon, in the months leading up to the fatal lunch.

Patterson told the court she had accidentally served beef wellingtons containing death cap mushrooms to her lunch guests in July 2023. She raised the possibility that mushrooms she had foraged may have been in a Tupperware container which also contained store-bought dried mushrooms she said she had used in the beef wellington meal.

But the jury ultimately sided with the prosecution, finding Patterson had deliberately included death cap mushrooms in the infamous lunch meal with the intention of killing her four guests.

world.title: Ebola outbreak in Democratic Republic of the Congo now deadliest in country’s history
world.snippet: At least 2,325 people have died from the virus, according to official data, with outbreak on track to be biggest in history The Ebola out...
world.content:
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is now the deadliest in the country’s history, with at least 2,325 people dead, according to government data, surpassing the toll from the 2018-20 outbreak.

The DRC’s public health institute said confirmed cases had risen to 4,945, including 101 detected in the previous 24 hours.

The World Health Organization has said the outbreak is on track to surpass west Africa’s 2014-16 Ebola outbreak as the biggest in history. The 2014-16 outbreak resulted in 28,616 cases and 11,325 deaths across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone, according to WHO data.

On Friday, the UN said Ebola “is winning in the Democratic Republic of the Congo” and said the epidemic was killing one person every 30 minutes.

Six of DRC’s 26 provinces have been affected, mainly those along the country’s north-eastern border. More than 3,400 of the cases have been recorded in Ituri province, where the outbreak was first reported.

The latest numbers of confirmed cases of Ebola in the DRC have made this outbreak – the 17th in the country’s history – the fastest-growing in the known history of the virus. It took almost five months for the 2014-16 west Africa outbreak to reach 1,000 deaths, compared with more than 2,000 deaths in less than three months in this outbreak.

There are no approved vaccines or treatments yet for the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus that is responsible for the current surge in cases. Nonetheless, 1,000 people in the DRC have recovered from the infection, with 730 still in healthcare or isolation facilities.

Clinical trials of two possible treatments for the strain began last month in Ituri. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the WHO director general, said last week that two vaccines developed specifically for Bundibugyo were now being tested on people.

Thomas Parisch, a public health specialist recently deployed to the DRC with Médecins Sans Frontières, said: “Normally, as an outbreak progresses, the case fatality ratio should fall as contact tracing improves and patients are identified and treated earlier. Instead, we’re still seeing many cases detected very late, when treatment is less likely to succeed, with many identified only after they die in the community.”

Uganda has reported at least 20 cases, all in the capital, Kampala. The last case reported there was on 21 June and no community transmission has been recorded. The government declared the country Ebola-free on 28 July after the last Ebola patient, a Congolese national, was discharged on 16 July.

In May, the WHO declared the outbreak in the DRC and Uganda as a public health emergency of international concern. It said sequencing showed the outbreak had started months earlier, in February.

Ebola is transmitted to people from wild animals and then spreads in the human population through direct contact with the blood, secretions, organs or other body fluids of infected people, including dead bodies, and with contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding or clothing.

According to the WHO, symptoms can include fever, fatigue, malaise, muscle pain, headache and sore throat. These are followed by vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, rash and symptoms of impaired kidney and liver functions.

The response to this outbreak has been hampered by attacks on healthcare facilities, often fuelled by misinformation about safe burial practices, as well as strikes by some unpaid health workers. Decades of unrest and outside interference on traumatised communities, as well as poor health and road infrastructure have also complicated the picture.

More than 70% of people die in the community and not in health centres, said Mohamed Janabi, the WHO’s regional Africa director.

Jean-Paul Malo Lotsima, a civil society official in the Djugu area of Ituri, told the AFP news agency: “People prefer to be treated at home, thinking it is a case of poisoning or some other illness.”

He added: “It’s often at the last minute, when the family realises that the situation is getting worse, that patients are taken to hospital. And sometimes, they die on the way.”

Flavier Ngurima, who lives in Nizi, one of the hotspots of the outbreak in Ituri, said his brother died before reaching the treatment centre. “We had called on a nurse from the family to treat him at home because the patient and the family members were afraid to go to the ETC [treatment centre],” he said. “They said that over there, a lot of people die.”

world.title: Zimbabwe boat accident death toll hits 68 as 22 more bodies recovered
world.snippet: Eighteen children among the people killed after ferry capsized on Lake Kariba Twenty-two more bodies have been recovered after a boat acc...
world.content:
Twenty-two more bodies have been recovered after a boat accident in Zimbabwe, taking the death toll to 68, police said on Saturday.

The ferry capsized on Tuesday on Lake Kariba, on the border with Zambia. An investigation has suggested it was overloaded when it turned over during heavy winds.

Eighteen children were among the people killed, Zimbabwe’s police said, in what is believed to be the country’s deadliest such disaster.

Most of the passengers are believed to be villagers and fish traders who lived around the lake.

Officials said the vessel was authorised to carry 90 people but was packed with 114 adults, five crew members and an unspecified number of children.

Lt Col Joseph Muchechesi, commander of the boat regiment involved in the search operation, said: “So far today we have managed to take 22 bodies. We are confident that we will manage to retrieve all the bodies.”

The civil protection unit said on Wednesday that 77 people had been rescued.

Hundreds of people gathered at the district hospital in the lakeside town of Kariba to identify the bodies of their relatives and loved ones.

A public memorial service was held in Kariba, nearly 280km (175 miles) north-west of the capital Harare, on Thursday before the burials started.

Survivors said they pleaded with the ferry driver to turn back as the vessel had begun taking on water soon after departing.

Chance Siyamavhu, 45, told Agence France-Presse: “Thank God that a wave pushed the sinking vessel and we managed to climb on top.

“When the boat capsized, most of the people scrambled to get the lifejackets but most of them did not even know how to use them.

“Most people could not make it.”

Lake Kariba is the world’s largest manmade lake by volume. It stretches more than 200km (124 miles) and is up to 40km (25 miles) wide in places.

It was created in the 1950s during British colonial rule, when the Zambezi River was dammed, displacing about 57,000 people.

In 2014, 26 people, 24 of them children, drowned in Zambia’s part of the lake, when the boat meant to transport them to independence day celebrations capsized.

On the Zimbabwean side, five passengers drowned in a 2021 incident.

world.title: Moroccan police arrest more than 100 people attempting to enter Ceuta
world.snippet: Border security tightened after social media posts call for another mass crossing into Spain’s north African territory Moroccan police ha...
world.content:
Moroccan police have arrested 111 people as they tried to enter Spain’s north African territory of Ceuta, amid ⁠tightened security on both sides after social media posts ​called for another mass crossing.

The attempted crossing on Saturday came two weeks after more than 72,000 migrants surged into Ceuta, causing tensions within the EU and prompting anti-immigration rhetoric among far-right parties worldwide. At least 96 people died trying to ⁠reach European soil.

A source in Morocco’s interior ministry told news agency Reuters that those detained included 109 migrants from sub-Saharan Africa and two Moroccan citizens arrested in or around Fnideq, the Moroccan city near Ceuta.

Moroccan police used teargas to disperse groups of migrants ⁠gathered on hills about 1.9 miles (3km) from the border, according to Spanish news agency EFE. Reuters later saw hundreds of police officers, some in riot gear and others in plainclothes, returning from the hills outside ​Fnideq.

EFE and Spanish state broadcaster TVE said Morocco’s interior ministry ordered their journalists ‌to leave Fnideq immediately, without providing an explanation.

In Ceuta, ‌Spanish soldiers guarded supermarkets while police patrolled the main streets. The city was calmer than in the days after the deadly crossing attempt on 30 July.

Madrid has ‌since installed a maritime barrier and deployed more than 500 additional police officers from mainland Spain, raising the total in Ceuta to more than 1,600. The interior ministry said the reinforcements would remain for as long as needed.

“We’ll continue to deploy whatever personnel are necessary to restore normality as soon as possible and prevent events like those of 30 July from happening again,” Spain’s interior minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, said on Thursday.

About 5,000 migrants remained in Ceuta, the minister added. Reuters saw hundreds sheltering from scorching heat under makeshift bamboo shelters on the urban beach of El Trampolin.

Grande-Marlaska said migrants who entered irregularly would not be allowed to stay in the territory, travel to mainland Spain or ‌obtain legal status, except in rare cases involving extreme vulnerability. Those without a right to remain would be returned to Morocco, he added.

Earlier this week, Rabat said it was monitoring “the circulation of social media posts and messages of unknown origin” calling for a mass crossing ​on 15 August, warning it would prosecute organisers and participants.

A Reuters witness saw reinforced security near the border, including police vans with wire shields and road checkpoints. Local media reported similar measures near Melilla, another Spanish territory in north Africa.

Authorities prevented several groups from boarding trains and buses to northern Morocco in cities such as Casablanca, Fez and Kenitra. However, witnesses told Reuters that some migrants from sub-Saharan Africa were bypassing security checkpoints by taking mountain routes towards Fnideq.

One witness said the schools in Fnideq had been turned into accommodation for security forces deployed near the ⁠border.

world.title: American missionary kidnapped in Niger freed after nine months
world.snippet: Kevin Rideout, who was abducted by unknown assailants in Niamey, said to be in good health and in care of US officials An American missio...
world.content:
An American missionary who was kidnapped in Niger in October has been released, his organisation has said.

Serving in Mission International said Kevin Rideout “is in good health in the care of US officials” and would soon be reunited with his extended family.

Donald Trump, who claimed to have helped secure Rideout’s release, later said he was “back in United States Custody” on Friday.

The 50-year-old missionary pilot was kidnapped in the west African country’s capital, Niamey, on 21 October by three armed individuals and was probably driven out of town, according to a security official at the time. No armed group claimed responsibility for the abduction. Other details about his rescue remain unknown.

The US president’s administration had made the release of Rideout a priority in its latest strategy on African Sahel states, after years of fighting extremism found limited success. Rideout had been working in Niger for 19 years as a missionary before the incident.

“I am proud to announce that Kevin Rideout, a wonderful Christian Missionary, is back in United States Custody,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform on Friday. “Kevin, the United States of America looks forward to welcoming you HOME. Glad to have helped!”

Niger has long been the target of attacks by armed groups, including jihadis linked to al-Qaida and Islamic State. A “continually deteriorating security situation” across the country was cited by the military junta that took power in 2023 when deposing the democratically elected president, Mohamed Bazoum.

The new authorities ousted western partners, including the US, which had soldiers in Niger, and forged a new security and diplomatic alliance with Russia. One former US base has since been occupied by Russian soldiers.

Trump described the broader region of west Africa as “the epicenter of Islamist terrorism” in his social media post on Friday, claiming there had been “more deadly attacks in the past year” there than anywhere else on Earth.

Washington has since shifted its focus to coastal west African states including Benin, Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana, sharing intelligence with local security personnel to prevent extremist threats from spilling southwards from the arid Sahel.

However, the insurgency continues to escalate in the region. In Niger, data from Acled, the armed conflict data aggregator, shows that civilian fatalities rose by nearly 50% in the year after Bazoum was ousted.

Cities and urban centres in the Sahel region have also been increasingly targeted by armed non-state actors as the crisis reaches new dimensions.

The US embassy in Niamey issued a security alert a day after Rideout’s abduction, warning that American citizens “remain at a heightened risk of kidnapping throughout Niger, including in the capital city”.

In June, more than 30 people were killed when gunmen attacked the main airport in Niamey. It was the second attack this year at the airport, a strategic hub that serves as the ruling military’s command, hosting its air force base and most of its drones and aircraft. It is also the headquarters of the Alliance of Sahel States, the regional alliance that brings together troops from Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso.

In April, Mali’s defence minister, Gen Sadio Camara, was killed in his home on the outskirts of the capital Bamako during coordinated assaults staged by insurgents including the west African affiliate of al-Qaida.

Associated Press and Agence France-Presse contributed reporting

world.title: DRC’s fast-growing Ebola outbreak spreads to sixth province
world.snippet: Man dies in Bas-Uele after travelling from Haut-Uele, as head of WHO says outbreak on track to be deadliest ever The Ebola outbreak in th...
world.content:
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has spread to a sixth province, officials have said, a day after the head of the World Health Organization said the outbreak was on track to surpass the deadliest in history, which killed at least 11,000 people more than a decade ago.

The current outbreak has killed more than 2,100 people out of more than 4,500 cases, according to the latest government figures released on Tuesday. At the same point in the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, the previous most deadly outbreak, 755 cases had been recorded, according to WHO data.

Jean Kaseya, the director general of Africa CDC, said on Thursday that a death had been recorded in the previously unaffected Bas-Uele province. The man had travelled from Isiro, in Haut-Uele province, to Buta, the capital of Bas-Uele, where he died, Kaseya said.

There are no approved vaccines or treatments for the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus that is responsible for the current outbreak.

The death toll has been reached almost three times faster than in the 2014-16 outbreak. On Wednesday, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the WHO director general, said the current outbreak would surpass that one based on its current pace.

Six of DRC’s 26 provinces have now been affected, mainly those along the country’s north-eastern border. More than 3,400 of the cases have been recorded in Ituri province, where the outbreak was first reported.

Uganda has reported 20 cases, all in the capital, Kampala. The last case there was reported on 21 June and no community transmission has been recorded.

The DRC outbreak is unfolding amid strikes by some unpaid health workers, global development aid cuts, threats by rebel groups, anger from long-traumatised communities, and misinformation claiming that Ebola is not real.

Health workers at the Nizi treatment centre in Ituri province went on strike on Thursday, leading to the temporary closure of the centre, saying they had not been paid for three months.

The true scope of the outbreak remains unknown. It was declared on 15 May but the WHO says sequencing now shows it began months earlier in February.

Health authorities have said between 60% and 70% of new cases are recorded outside contacts being monitored, and that the disease is spreading at an alarming rate.

Dr Mohamed Yakub Janabi, the WHO regional director for Africa, said this week: “We are chasing the virus; the virus is ahead of us.”

Nonetheless, his colleague Abdirahman Mahamud, the head of the WHO’s emergency response division, sounded a note of optimism on Wednesday, saying that if the pandemic response was implemented “at the same time across the five transmission zones, we are expecting a turnaround in three months”.

Even with that, Mahamud said the peak of the outbreak would not be reached for six months under a “moderate” scenario and that the outbreak could last nine to 12 months.

Ebola is rare but highly contagious and can be contracted from body fluids such as vomit, blood or semen, including from dead bodies, and from contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding and clothing. The disease it causes is severe and often fatal.

Clinical trials of two possible treatments for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola causing this outbreak began last month in Ituri. Tedros said on Wednesday two vaccines developed specifically for this strain were now being tested on people for the first time.

This strain of Bundibugyo is genetically different from previous outbreaks in 2007 and 2012, making it likely that this outbreak began when the virus jumped from an infected animal to a human, researchers said in a paper published this week in the journal Nature Medicine. They had sequenced genomes from samples from 22 people with Ebola.

Last week, Kaseya said officials were worried the virus could be mutating and that the Africa CDC was planning further studies with the WHO to investigate.

Associated Press and Agence France-Presse contributed to this story.
